Exercise 7. 1 The fire alarm sounded at 2 a.m. on Tuesday. 2 The night porter evacuated the guests from the east wing. 3 A chef burned his hand in the kitchen. 4 The receptionist called an ambulance immediately. 5 Nobody was seriously injured. 6 The duty manager wrote an incident report before the end of her shift.
Audio transcript — unit-14.mp3

Karim (Safety Officer): Good morning, everyone, and welcome to your first safety briefing at the Caravan Plaza Hotel in Samarkand. Lina, where is the nearest fire extinguisher to the front desk?

Lina (Trainee Receptionist): It's on the wall next to the luggage room, about three metres from my chair.

Karim (Safety Officer): Correct. Now listen carefully. If the fire alarm sounds, follow these steps. First, stay calm — guests will copy your behaviour. Second, pick up the red emergency folder under the printer and take the guest list with you. Then lead the guests down the stairs — never use the lifts. Finally, count every guest at the assembly point.

Diego (Trainee Porter): Where exactly is the assembly point?

Karim (Safety Officer): Good question, Diego. It's in the rose garden, twenty metres from the main entrance, away from the building. Lina, what will you do if a guest is injured?

Lina (Trainee Receptionist): I'll call an ambulance on 103, and I'll give first aid if it is safe to do so.

Karim (Safety Officer): Exactly. The first-aid kit is behind reception, and there is a defibrillator in the lobby. One last thing: we hold a fire drill on the first Monday of every month, so the next one is in five days. Now let's walk the evacuation route together.

Exercise 19.
Model answer: Incident Report. Date and time: 12 May, 16:05. Location: Chorsu Guesthouse courtyard, Tashkent. People involved: Mr Daniel Okoro, a guest from Nigeria, and two staff members. What occurred: Mr Okoro slipped on a wet step and injured his knee. A waiter witnessed the fall and reported it immediately. How staff responded: the receptionist called 103, and a trained first-aider treated the injury. Injuries and damage: one minor knee injury; no damage to property. Recommendation: if we fit a handrail and a warning sign on the steps, similar accidents will not occur again.
Exercise 20.
Model answer: ROOM SAFETY CARD — Caravan Plaza Hotel. Read this card when you arrive. Keep your room key with you at all times. Do not smoke in the room — every room has a smoke detector. Do not use candles or cooking equipment. If the fire alarm sounds, you will see green exit signs in the corridor — follow them to the stairs. If you need urgent medical help, dial 0 for reception and we will call an ambulance. Assembly point: the rose garden, twenty metres from the main entrance.
126
GLOSSARY

This glossary brings together every key word and phrase taught in the fourteen units of A Complete Guide to Tourism English. Entries are listed alphabetically; each one shows the word, its pronunciation in the International Phonetic Alphabet, its part of speech (n. noun, v. verb, adj. adjective, phr. phrase), a simple definition, an example sentence from a tourism context, and the unit where the word first appears. Use it to revise before tests, to check a meaning while you work through an activity, or to return to the unit where a word is practised in full.

accommodation /əˌkɒməˈdeɪʃn/ n. a place to stay, such as a hotel, hostel or guesthouse. e.g. The tour price includes accommodation and breakfast. (Unit 1)
adventure tourism /ədˈventʃə ˈtʊərɪzəm/ n. tourism with exciting outdoor activities such as climbing or rafting. e.g. Adventure tourism takes visitors into the mountains and the desert. (Unit 1)
affordable /əˈfɔːdəbl/ adj. cheap enough for most people to pay for. e.g. Hostels are an affordable choice for young travellers. (Unit 2)
agenda /əˈdʒendə/ n. the list of topics or sessions planned for a meeting or conference. e.g. Please find attached the agenda for Friday's seminar. (Unit 13)
all-inclusive /ˌɔːl ɪnˈkluːsɪv/ adj. with meals, drinks and most activities included in one single price. e.g. Their all-inclusive package covers every meal and two guided excursions. (Unit 12)
allergy /ˈælədʒi/ n. a medical reaction to a food such as nuts, milk or eggs. e.g. One guest had a serious nut allergy, so we informed the chef. (Unit 5)
amenities /əˈmiːnətiz/ n. useful or pleasant extras that make a stay more comfortable, such as Wi-Fi or toiletries. e.g. Free Wi-Fi and air conditioning are standard amenities here. (Unit 2)
ancient /ˈeɪnʃənt/ adj. extremely old; from the distant past. e.g. Tourists wander through the ancient streets of the walled city. (Unit 10)
anecdote /ˈænɪkdəʊt/ n. a short, amusing true story about a real person or event. e.g. He told a funny anecdote about a sultan and his cook. (Unit 9)
apologize /əˈpɒlədʒaɪz/ v. to say that you are sorry for a problem or mistake. e.g. The receptionist apologized for the noisy neighbours. (Unit 7)
archway /ˈɑːtʃweɪ/ n. an entrance or passage under a curved arch. e.g. We passed through a tall stone archway into the inner city. (Unit 10)
assembly point /əˈsembli pɔɪnt/ n. a safe place outside a building where everyone must gather during an evacuation. e.g. Our assembly point is the car park opposite the main entrance. (Unit 14)
attract /əˈtrækt/ v. to make people want to come to a place or use a service. e.g. The new night market attracts thousands of visitors every weekend. (Unit 12)
audience /ˈɔːdiəns/ n. the group of people who are listening to a speaker. e.g. A good guide watches the audience and notices when they are tired. (Unit 9)
availability /əˌveɪləˈbɪləti/ n. the rooms, seats or places that are still free to book. e.g. Let me check availability for the tenth of July. (Unit 3)
award-winning /əˈwɔːd wɪnɪŋ/ adj. having won one or more prizes for being excellent. e.g. Our award-winning spa was named the best in the region last year. (Unit 12)
B&B (bed and breakfast) /ˌbiː ən ˈbiː/ n. a small private house or guesthouse that offers a room for the night and breakfast in the morning. e.g. We stayed at a friendly B&B near the lake. (Unit 2)
bargain /ˈbɑːɡən/ v. to discuss a price with a seller in order to pay less. e.g. At Siyob Bazaar you can bargain politely over the price of dried fruit. (Unit 11)
bazaar /bəˈzɑː(r)/ n. a large market, especially in Asia, where many traders sell goods. e.g. You can buy silk scarves and fresh spices at the bazaar. (Unit 6)
between /bɪˈtwiːn/ phr. in the space that separates two places. e.g. The information centre is between the bank and the post office. (Unit 6)
beverage /ˈbevərɪdʒ/ n. any kind of drink, hot or cold. e.g. Hot beverages such as tea and coffee are free at breakfast. (Unit 5)
book /bʊk/ v. to reserve a room, ticket or tour in advance. e.g. We booked three nights at the Emir Hotel. (Unit 3)
book in advance /bʊk ɪn ədˈvɑːns/ phr. to reserve something early, before the date you need it. e.g. In peak season you should book in advance to get the best rooms. (Unit 12)
booking /ˈbʊkɪŋ/ n. a reservation for a room, a ticket or a tour. e.g. The receptionist takes bookings by phone and online. (Unit 1)
booking reference /ˈbʊkɪŋ ˈrefrəns/ n. the letters and numbers that identify a reservation. e.g. Your booking reference is NT-4172. (Unit 3)
bow /baʊ/ v. to bend your head or body forward to greet somebody or show respect. e.g. The guide taught us to bow slightly when we met the elders of the village. (Unit 11)
breakout room /ˈbreɪkaʊt ruːm/ n. a smaller room used for group sessions away from the main conference hall. e.g. Workshop B is taking place in the largest breakout room. (Unit 13)
breathtaking /ˈbreθteɪkɪŋ/ adj. extremely beautiful or impressive, almost making you stop breathing. e.g. The view from the watchtower at sunset is absolutely breathtaking. (Unit 10)
bridge /brɪdʒ/ n. a structure that carries a road or path over a river. e.g. Cross the bridge and the park is on your right. (Unit 6)
brochure /ˈbrəʊʃə/ n. a thin magazine with pictures that advertises a product, holiday or place. e.g. She picked up a brochure about Silk Road tours at the travel fair. (Unit 12)
buffet /ˈbʊfeɪ/ n. a meal where guests serve themselves from a long table of dishes. e.g. The breakfast buffet opens at seven o'clock. (Unit 5)
business travel /ˈbɪznəs ˌtrævl/ n. travelling to meetings, conferences and other work events. e.g. Business travel brings many visitors to the capital city. (Unit 1)
call back /ˌkɔːl ˈbæk/ phr. to phone somebody again at a later time. e.g. Mr Lee is out of the office. Could you call back after lunch? (Unit 8)
caller /ˈkɔːlə/ n. the person who makes a telephone call. e.g. Always ask the caller for their name and number. (Unit 8)
campaign /kæmˈpeɪn/ n. a planned series of advertisements with one clear goal. e.g. The airline launched a winter campaign to attract more passengers. (Unit 12)
cancel /ˈkænsl/ v. to say that a planned booking will not happen. e.g. She had to cancel her trip to Bukhara. (Unit 3)
cancellation policy /ˌkænsəˈleɪʃn ˈpɒləsi/ n. the rules about returning money when a guest does not travel. e.g. Read the cancellation policy carefully before you pay. (Unit 3)
catering /ˈkeɪtərɪŋ/ n. the service of providing food and drink at an event. e.g. The catering for the gala dinner includes a full vegetarian menu. (Unit 13)
charge /tʃɑːdʒ/ v. to take money from someone as payment. e.g. We won't charge your card before May. (Unit 3)
check in /ˌtʃek ˈɪn/ v. to arrive at a hotel, give your details and receive your room. e.g. You can check in any time after two o'clock. (Unit 4)
check out /ˌtʃek ˈaʊt/ v. to pay your bill and leave the hotel at the end of your stay. e.g. We have to check out before twelve o'clock. (Unit 4)
check-in date /ˈtʃekɪn deɪt/ n. the day a guest arrives and a stay begins. e.g. Choose your check-in date and the number of nights. (Unit 3)
chef /ʃef/ n. a professional cook in a hotel or restaurant kitchen. e.g. The chef cooks plov for two hundred guests every day. (Unit 1)
citadel /ˈsɪtədəl/ n. a fortress that protects a city, usually built on high ground. e.g. The ancient citadel rises on a hill above the river. (Unit 10)
clear /klɪə/ v. to take empty plates and glasses away from a table. e.g. Please clear table six before the next group arrives. (Unit 5)
code word /ˈkəʊd wɜːd/ n. a word such as Alpha or Bravo used to make a letter clear when spelling on the phone. e.g. Use code words when you spell a guest's surname over the phone. (Unit 8)
cold meal /kəʊld miːl/ n. food that is served cold when it should be hot. e.g. The waiter took the cold meal back to the kitchen and apologized. (Unit 7)
commentary /ˈkɒməntri/ n. the spoken information a guide gives during a tour. e.g. Her lively commentary made the bus tour unforgettable. (Unit 9)
compensation /ˌkɒmpenˈseɪʃn/ n. money or gifts given to a customer to make a bad situation better. e.g. As compensation, the airline offered a free flight voucher. (Unit 7)
complain /kəmˈpleɪn/ v. to say that you are not happy or satisfied with something. e.g. Mr Becker complained about the noise at the front desk. (Unit 7)
complaint /kəmˈpleɪnt/ n. a statement that you are not happy with a product or service. e.g. The front desk received a complaint about the leaking tap. (Unit 7)
complimentary /ˌkɒmplɪˈmentri/ adj. given free of charge to a guest or customer. e.g. Every booking includes a complimentary airport transfer. (Unit 12)
concierge /ˌkɒnsiˈeəʒ/ n. a hotel employee who helps guests with tours, taxis, restaurants and tickets. e.g. The concierge booked theatre tickets for the guests. (Unit 2)
conference /ˈkɒnfərəns/ n. a large formal meeting where people with shared professional interests listen to talks and exchange ideas. e.g. Over 300 delegates attended the tourism conference in Tashkent. (Unit 13)
127
GLOSSARY

(continued: confirm – host)

confirm /kənˈfɜːm/ v. to say officially that a booking is fixed. e.g. Shall I confirm the booking now? (Unit 3)
confirmation /ˌkɒnfəˈmeɪʃn/ n. a message that shows a booking was successful. e.g. Your confirmation will arrive by email this afternoon. (Unit 3)
cosy /ˈkəʊzi/ adj. small, warm and comfortable, like a home. e.g. The guesthouse has got a cosy tea room beside the garden. (Unit 2)
courtesy /ˈkɜːtəsi/ n. polite behaviour that shows respect for other people. e.g. Standing up to greet an older guest is a simple act of courtesy. (Unit 11)
courtyard /ˈkɔːtjɑːd/ n. an open space inside a building or between walls, without a roof. e.g. Students once lived in the small rooms around the shady courtyard. (Unit 10)
credit card /ˈkredɪt kɑːd/ n. a bank card used to pay for things now and pay the bank later. e.g. Can I pay the deposit by credit card? (Unit 3)
crossroads /ˈkrɒsrəʊdz/ n. a place where two roads meet and cross each other. e.g. At the crossroads, go straight ahead. (Unit 6)
cultural tourism /ˈkʌltʃərəl ˈtʊərɪzəm/ n. tourism that focuses on museums, festivals and historic places. e.g. Cultural tourism is very popular along the Silk Road. (Unit 1)
custom /ˈkʌstəm/ n. a traditional way of behaving that is special to a place, group or culture. e.g. Offering guests green tea before a meal is an old custom in Central Asia. (Unit 11)
day trip /ˈdeɪ trɪp/ n. a visit to a place that you start and finish on the same day. e.g. Samarkand is an easy day trip from Tashkent by fast train. (Unit 9)
deal /diːl/ n. an agreement or offer, especially one with a good price. e.g. Two excursions for the price of one — what a deal! (Unit 12)
defibrillator /diːˈfɪbrɪleɪtə/ n. an electronic machine that can restart a person's heart in a medical emergency. e.g. There is a defibrillator on the wall behind the reception desk. (Unit 14)
delegate /ˈdelɪɡət/ n. a person who attends a conference, often representing a company or organisation. e.g. Each delegate received a printed programme at the entrance. (Unit 13)
deposit /dɪˈpɒzɪt/ n. part of the price paid first to hold a booking. e.g. The hotel asks for a 20 per cent deposit by card. (Unit 3)
dessert /dɪˈzɜːt/ n. sweet food eaten at the end of a meal. e.g. The chocolate cake is our most popular dessert. (Unit 5)
destination /ˌdestɪˈneɪʃn/ n. a place that people travel to for a holiday or a trip. e.g. Samarkand is a popular destination for cultural tourists. (Unit 1)
dial /ˈdaɪəl/ v. to press the numbers on a phone in order to call somebody. e.g. Dial 0 for reception from any room in the hotel. (Unit 8)
discount /ˈdɪskaʊnt/ n. an amount of money taken off the normal price. e.g. Students get a 15% discount on all our city tours. (Unit 12)
dome /dəʊm/ n. a rounded roof on top of a building. e.g. The turquoise dome of the mausoleum can be seen from across the city. (Unit 10)
double room /ˌdʌbl ˈruːm/ n. a hotel room with one large bed for two people. e.g. The couple booked a double room with a city view. (Unit 2)
dress code /ˈdres kəʊd/ n. the rules about what you may or may not wear in a particular place. e.g. The mosque has a strict dress code, so visitors must cover their shoulders. (Unit 11)
ecotourism /ˈiːkəʊˌtʊərɪzəm/ n. tourism that protects nature and helps local communities. e.g. Ecotourism is growing fast in the Nuratau Mountains. (Unit 1)
emergency exit /ɪˈmɜːdʒənsi ˌeksɪt/ n. a special door used to leave a building quickly in a dangerous situation. e.g. The emergency exit on the third floor is at the end of the corridor. (Unit 14)
en-suite /ˌɒn ˈswiːt/ adj. (of a bathroom) connected directly to the bedroom. e.g. Every double room is en-suite, so guests never share a bathroom. (Unit 2)
engaged /ɪnˈɡeɪdʒd/ adj. (of a phone line) busy because somebody is already using it. e.g. Her line is engaged at the moment. Would you like to hold? (Unit 8)
enquire /ɪnˈkwaɪə/ v. to ask formally for information. e.g. I am writing to enquire about your conference packages. (Unit 13)
etiquette /ˈetɪket/ n. the formal rules of polite behaviour in a society or profession. e.g. Hotel staff study international etiquette so they never embarrass a guest. (Unit 11)
evacuate /ɪˈvækjueɪt/ v. to move people out of a dangerous place to a safe one. e.g. Staff evacuated the restaurant calmly and quickly. (Unit 14)
evacuation /ɪˌvækjuˈeɪʃn/ n. the process of moving people out of a dangerous building or area. e.g. The evacuation of the beach resort took less than ten minutes. (Unit 14)
exclusive /ɪkˈskluːsɪv/ adj. available only to a small, special group of people. e.g. This exclusive offer is for newsletter readers only. (Unit 12)
excursion /ɪkˈskɜːʃn/ n. a short organized trip, usually for a group, to visit an interesting place. e.g. The hotel offers an excursion to the mountain lake every Friday. (Unit 9)
exhibition stand /ˌeksɪˈbɪʃn stænd/ n. a display area where a company shows its products or services at a fair. e.g. Our travel agency booked an exhibition stand near the main entrance. (Unit 13)
extension /ɪkˈstenʃn/ n. an internal telephone number inside a company or hotel. e.g. You can reach the spa on extension 24. (Unit 8)
facilities /fəˈsɪlətiz/ n. the rooms, equipment and services that a hotel offers its guests. e.g. The resort's facilities include a spa, a gym and two restaurants. (Unit 2)
faulty /ˈfɔːlti/ adj. not working correctly. e.g. The air conditioning in our room was faulty, so the room was too hot. (Unit 7)
fire alarm /ˈfaɪər əˌlɑːm/ n. a bell or siren that warns people in a building about a fire. e.g. If the fire alarm sounds, guests must leave the building immediately. (Unit 14)
fire drill /ˈfaɪə drɪl/ n. a regular practice of what to do during a fire. e.g. The hotel holds a fire drill on the first Monday of every month. (Unit 14)
fire extinguisher /ˈfaɪər ɪkˌstɪŋɡwɪʃə/ n. a metal container of water, foam or powder used to put out a small fire. e.g. Every hotel kitchen must have a fire extinguisher on the wall. (Unit 14)
first-aid kit /ˌfɜːst ˈeɪd kɪt/ n. a box of bandages, plasters and medicines for treating minor injuries. e.g. The tour guide carries a first-aid kit on every mountain excursion. (Unit 14)
flight attendant /ˈflaɪt əˌtendənt/ n. a person who looks after passengers during a flight. e.g. The flight attendant serves drinks and meals on the plane. (Unit 1)
fortress /ˈfɔːtrəs/ n. a large, strong building made to defend a town in the past. e.g. The ancient fortress stands on a hill above the river. (Unit 9)
fountain /ˈfaʊntɪn/ n. a structure that sends water up into the air, often found in squares and parks. e.g. Turn left at the fountain and keep walking. (Unit 6)
front desk /ˌfrʌnt ˈdesk/ n. the counter in a hotel lobby where guests check in and check out. e.g. Please leave your key card at the front desk when you leave. (Unit 4)
gesture /ˈdʒestʃə/ n. a movement of the hands or head that shows a feeling or meaning. e.g. Pointing with one finger is a rude gesture in many cultures. (Unit 11)
gluten-free /ˌɡluːtən friː/ adj. containing no gluten; safe for guests who cannot eat wheat. e.g. We bake gluten-free bread for guests with a wheat intolerance. (Unit 5)
go past /gəʊ pɑːst/ phr. to walk by a place without stopping. e.g. Go past the museum and take the next street. (Unit 6)
go straight ahead /gəʊ streɪt əˈhed/ phr. to continue walking or driving in the same direction without turning. e.g. Go straight ahead until you reach the fountain. (Unit 6)
greeting /ˈɡriːtɪŋ/ n. a word or action used to welcome somebody when you meet them. e.g. A warm greeting in the local language always makes a good first impression. (Unit 11)
guest /ɡest/ n. a person who is staying at a hotel. e.g. Zarina has checked in more than sixty guests this week. (Unit 4)
guesthouse /ˈɡesthaʊs/ n. a small, family-run place to stay, usually cheaper than a hotel. e.g. The guesthouse in Khiva serves breakfast in its courtyard. (Unit 2)
halal /həˈlɑːl/ adj. prepared according to Islamic dietary law. e.g. Guests from Malaysia often ask if the lamb is halal. (Unit 5)
handshake /ˈhændʃeɪk/ n. the act of holding and shaking somebody's hand as a greeting. e.g. In Germany, a firm handshake is the normal way to open a business meeting. (Unit 11)
hang up /ˌhæŋ ˈʌp/ phr. to end a phone call by putting the receiver down. e.g. In good service, you never hang up before the caller does. (Unit 8)
hazard /ˈhæzəd/ n. anything that could be dangerous or cause an accident. e.g. A wet lobby floor is a serious hazard for elderly guests. (Unit 14)
headcount /ˈhedkaʊnt/ n. the act of counting the people in a group. e.g. The guide did a quick headcount before the bus left. (Unit 9)
headset /ˈhedset/ n. headphones with a small microphone, used for hands-free calls. e.g. The booking agents wear headsets so they can type while they talk. (Unit 8)
hold the line /ˌhəʊld ðə ˈlaɪn/ phr. to wait on the phone without hanging up. e.g. Hold the line, please. I'll check if the manager is free. (Unit 8)
hospitality /ˌhɒspɪˈtæləti/ n. the friendly and generous treatment of guests and visitors. e.g. Uzbek hospitality means a guest never leaves the table hungry. (Unit 11)
host /həʊst/ n. a person who invites guests and looks after them in their home. e.g. Our host filled every cup of tea himself, as tradition requires. (Unit 11)
host /həʊst/ v. to organise an event and provide the place for it. e.g. Our ballroom hosts up to five conferences every month. (Unit 13)
128
GLOSSARY

(continued: hostel – rate)

hostel /ˈhɒstəl/ n. cheap accommodation where travellers often share bedrooms and bathrooms. e.g. A bed in the city hostel costs only fifteen dollars a night. (Unit 2)
hotel manager /həʊˈtel ˈmænɪdʒə/ n. the person who is responsible for everything in a hotel. e.g. The hotel manager checks the rooms every morning. (Unit 1)
iconic /aɪˈkɒnɪk/ adj. very famous and considered a symbol of a place or idea. e.g. The Eiffel Tower is the most iconic landmark in France. (Unit 10)
in front of /ɪn frʌnt ɒv/ phr. directly before something, facing it. e.g. A taxi rank is in front of the railway station. (Unit 6)
in my opinion /ɪn maɪ əˈpɪnjən/ phr. a phrase used to show that what you are saying is your personal view. e.g. In my opinion, every guide should learn the basic customs of their visitors. (Unit 11)
inconvenience /ˌɪnkənˈviːniəns/ n. something that causes you problems or extra trouble. e.g. We are sorry for the inconvenience caused by the power cut. (Unit 7)
injure /ˈɪndʒə/ v. to hurt a person's body, for example in an accident. e.g. Two passengers were slightly injured when the coach braked suddenly. (Unit 14)
invoice /ˈɪnvɔɪs/ n. a document that lists services and the money a customer must pay. e.g. The agent will email the invoice today. (Unit 3)
itinerary /aɪˈtɪnərəri/ n. a detailed plan of a journey, with times, places and activities. e.g. Please read the itinerary carefully before our day trip tomorrow. (Unit 9)
key card /ˈkiː kɑːd/ n. a plastic card that opens the door of a hotel room. e.g. The receptionist gave Mr. Tanaka the key card for room 412. (Unit 4)
keynote speaker /ˈkiːnəʊt ˈspiːkə/ n. the main invited speaker who opens a conference with the most important talk. e.g. The keynote speaker is arriving at nine o'clock tomorrow morning. (Unit 13)
landmark /ˈlændmɑːk/ n. a famous building or place that is easy to see and recognise. e.g. Use the TV tower as a landmark when you explore the city. (Unit 6)
leaking tap /ˈliːkɪŋ tæp/ n. a tap that drips water even when it is turned off. e.g. The leaking tap in room 12 kept the guest awake all night. (Unit 7)
legend /ˈledʒənd/ n. an old story about a place or person that may not be completely true. e.g. Every stone of this fortress has its own legend. (Unit 9)
lift /lɪft/ n. a machine that carries people up and down between floors (US: elevator). e.g. The lift was broken, so we carried our bags up five floors. (Unit 7)
limited availability /ˌlɪmɪtɪd əˌveɪləˈbɪləti/ phr. only a small number of rooms, seats or places left to sell. e.g. Book soon — the desert camp has limited availability in May. (Unit 12)
lobby /ˈlɒbi/ n. the entrance hall of a hotel where guests arrive and wait. e.g. There are comfortable sofas and a piano in the lobby. (Unit 2)
look forward to /lʊk ˈfɔːwəd tuː/ phr. a polite phrase used to say that you are waiting for something with pleasure. e.g. I look forward to hearing from you. (Unit 13)
lost luggage /lɒst ˈlʌɡɪdʒ/ n. bags or suitcases that do not arrive with the traveller. e.g. She reported her lost luggage at the airline desk. (Unit 7)
low season /ləʊ ˈsiːzn/ n. the quiet time of year when travel is cheaper. e.g. November is low season in Khiva, so rooms are cheap. (Unit 3)
luggage /ˈlʌɡɪdʒ/ n. the bags and suitcases a traveller carries on a trip. e.g. Would you like some help with your luggage? (Unit 4)
luggage trolley /ˈlʌɡɪdʒ ˌtrɒli/ n. a small cart on wheels used for moving heavy bags inside a hotel. e.g. Bekzod put the three suitcases on a luggage trolley. (Unit 4)
luxurious /lʌɡˈʒʊəriəs/ adj. very expensive, elegant and extremely comfortable. e.g. The presidential suite is the most luxurious room in the hotel. (Unit 2)
magnificent /mæɡˈnɪfɪsənt/ adj. extremely impressive and beautiful, especially in a grand way. e.g. The square is surrounded by three magnificent madrasahs. (Unit 10)
main course /meɪn kɔːs/ n. the largest and most important dish of a meal. e.g. For the main course, David chose grilled lamb with rice. (Unit 5)
mausoleum /ˌmɔːsəˈliːəm/ n. a grand building that contains the tomb of an important person. e.g. The emperor's mausoleum is visited by thousands of people every day. (Unit 10)
meeting point /ˈmiːtɪŋ pɔɪnt/ n. the place where a group agrees to meet before or during a tour. e.g. Our meeting point is the fountain in front of the hotel. (Unit 9)
menu /ˈmenjuː/ n. a list of the dishes and drinks available in a restaurant. e.g. The waiter handed each guest a menu. (Unit 5)
message pad /ˈmesɪdʒ pæd/ n. a small block of paper for writing down callers' messages. e.g. Keep a message pad and a pen next to every phone at reception. (Unit 8)
minaret /ˌmɪnəˈret/ n. a tall, slim tower that stands beside a mosque. e.g. Visitors climb the minaret for a panoramic view of the old town. (Unit 10)
modest /ˈmɒdɪst/ adj. (of clothes) covering the body and not designed to attract attention. e.g. Modest clothing is required inside the cathedral and the old madrasah. (Unit 11)
monument /ˈmɒnjumənt/ n. a statue or building that reminds people of a famous person or event. e.g. The monument to the poet stands in front of the theatre. (Unit 6)
mosaic /məʊˈzeɪɪk/ n. a picture or pattern made of small pieces of coloured tile, stone or glass. e.g. The walls of the madrasah are decorated with blue and gold mosaics. (Unit 10)
mosque /mɒsk/ n. a building where Muslims pray. e.g. The old mosque is next to the tallest minaret in the city. (Unit 6)
name badge /ˈneɪm bædʒ/ n. a small card with a person's name and company, worn at business events. e.g. Please collect your name badge at the registration desk. (Unit 13)
networking /ˈnetwɜːkɪŋ/ n. meeting people at events in order to build useful professional contacts. e.g. The evening reception on the terrace is perfect for networking. (Unit 13)
next to /nekst tuː/ phr. directly beside something, with nothing in between. e.g. The café is next to the bookshop. (Unit 6)
noisy neighbours /ˈnɔɪzi ˈneɪbəz/ n. people in the next room or house who make too much noise. e.g. We couldn't sleep because of the noisy neighbours upstairs. (Unit 7)
occur /əˈkɜː/ v. to happen, often unexpectedly (formal). e.g. The power cut occurred at 11.40 p.m. during the storm. (Unit 14)
offend /əˈfend/ v. to make somebody upset or angry, especially by being rude to them. e.g. Tour leaders explain local rules so that visitors do not offend their hosts. (Unit 11)
on the corner of /ɒn ðə ˈkɔːnə(r) ɒv/ phr. at the place where two streets meet. e.g. The pharmacy is on the corner of Silk Street and Main Street. (Unit 6)
opposite /ˈɒpəzɪt/ phr. directly on the other side of a street or space from something. e.g. The bazaar is opposite the mosque. (Unit 6)
order /ˈɔːdə/ v. to ask for food or drink in a restaurant. e.g. The tourists ordered two starters and one dessert to share. (Unit 5)
ornate /ɔːˈneɪt/ adj. decorated with many complicated patterns and details. e.g. The portal of the mausoleum is covered in ornate tilework. (Unit 10)
overbooking /ˌəʊvəˈbʊkɪŋ/ n. selling more rooms or seats than are really available. e.g. Because of overbooking, two guests had no room when they arrived. (Unit 7)
package tour /ˈpækɪdʒ tʊə/ n. a holiday arranged by a company that includes transport, hotels and tours for one price. e.g. Their package tour included flights, meals and three guided tours. (Unit 9)
pass on /ˌpɑːs ˈɒn/ phr. to give a message to the person it is for. e.g. I'll pass your message on to the guide right away. (Unit 8)
passenger /ˈpæsɪndʒə/ n. a person who travels on a plane, bus, train or ship. e.g. The flight attendant helps every passenger find a seat. (Unit 1)
passport /ˈpɑːspɔːt/ n. an official document that proves who you are and lets you travel to other countries. e.g. Could I see your passport, please? (Unit 4)
peak season /piːk ˈsiːzn/ n. the busiest and most expensive time of year for travel. e.g. Rates almost double in the peak season. (Unit 3)
point out /pɔɪnt aʊt/ phr. to show something to people by directing their attention to it. e.g. The guide pointed out the carved doors that tourists usually miss. (Unit 9)
porter /ˈpɔːtə/ n. a hotel employee who carries guests' bags to and from their rooms. e.g. The porter has already taken your suitcase upstairs. (Unit 4)
pour /pɔː/ v. to make a liquid flow from a bottle or teapot into a glass or cup. e.g. She poured green tea into the small cups. (Unit 5)
power cut /ˈpaʊə kʌt/ n. a period of time when there is no electricity. e.g. A power cut stopped the lifts for almost an hour. (Unit 7)
projector /prəˈdʒektə/ n. a machine that shows slides or video on a large screen. e.g. The projector in the ballroom connects to laptops and tablets. (Unit 13)
promote /prəˈməʊt/ v. to advertise something in order to increase its sales or popularity. e.g. The tourism board promotes the region at fairs all over the world. (Unit 12)
punctuality /ˌpʌŋktʃuˈæləti/ n. the habit of arriving or doing things exactly at the agreed time. e.g. In Switzerland, punctuality is treated as a basic form of respect. (Unit 11)
put through /ˌpʊt ˈθruː/ phr. to connect a caller to another person or extension. e.g. One moment, please. I'll put you through to the tours department. (Unit 8)
quotation /kwəʊˈteɪʃn/ n. a formal document stating the price of a service. e.g. The events coordinator is sending the quotation this afternoon. (Unit 13)
rate /reɪt/ n. the price charged for a room or service, often per night. e.g. The nightly rate includes breakfast. (Unit 3)
129
GLOSSARY

(continued: receipt – witness)

receipt /rɪˈsiːt/ n. a piece of paper that proves you have paid for something. e.g. Keep the receipt in case you need it for your company. (Unit 4)
receiver /rɪˈsiːvə/ n. the part of a telephone that you hold to your ear and mouth. e.g. He picked up the receiver and dialled the travel agency. (Unit 8)
reception /rɪˈsepʃn/ n. the front desk of a hotel where guests check in and check out. e.g. Reception is open twenty-four hours a day. (Unit 2)
receptionist /rɪˈsepʃənɪst/ n. a person who welcomes guests at the front desk of a hotel. e.g. The receptionist gives every guest a key card and a smile. (Unit 1)
recommend /ˌrekəˈmend/ v. to tell a guest that a dish is good and worth ordering. e.g. I always recommend the pumpkin soup to new guests. (Unit 5)
refill /ˌriːˈfɪl/ v. to fill a glass or cup again. e.g. A good waiter refills the water glasses before guests ask. (Unit 5)
refund /ˈriːfʌnd/ n. money returned to a customer after a cancellation. e.g. You will receive a full refund if you cancel early. (Unit 3)
registration /ˌredʒɪˈstreɪʃn/ n. the process of signing in at the start of an event. e.g. Registration is opening at 8:30 in the hotel lobby. (Unit 13)
registration form /ˌredʒɪˈstreɪʃn fɔːm/ n. a document that guests fill in with their personal details when they arrive at a hotel. e.g. Could you fill in this registration form and sign at the bottom, please? (Unit 4)
replace /rɪˈpleɪs/ v. to change something old or broken for a new one. e.g. The maintenance team replaced the faulty air conditioner. (Unit 7)
report /rɪˈpɔːt/ v. to tell someone in authority about an accident or problem. e.g. Guests should report any hazard to the front desk at once. (Unit 14)
reservation /ˌrezəˈveɪʃn/ n. an arrangement to keep a room, seat or table for someone. e.g. I'd like to make a reservation for two nights, please. (Unit 3)
resort /rɪˈzɔːt/ n. a large holiday hotel complex with many leisure facilities, often by the sea or in the mountains. e.g. The Aqua Palm Resort has got three pools and a private beach. (Unit 2)
respond /rɪˈspɒnd/ v. to act quickly when something happens. e.g. The duty manager responded to the alarm within two minutes. (Unit 14)
restore /rɪˈstɔː/ v. to repair an old building or object so that it looks as it did originally. e.g. The damaged mosaics were restored by local craftsmen in 2019. (Unit 10)
room service /ˈruːm ˌsɜːvɪs/ n. food and drinks delivered straight to a guest's room. e.g. They ordered dinner from room service after the long flight. (Unit 2)
route /ruːt/ n. the way you follow to get from one place to another on a tour. e.g. The guide changed the route because of the road works. (Unit 9)
sacred /ˈseɪkrɪd/ adj. connected with religion and therefore treated with great respect. e.g. Visitors speak quietly inside the sacred shrine on the hill. (Unit 11)
seminar /ˈsemɪnɑː/ n. a meeting where a small group receives training or discusses a special topic. e.g. The hotel is hosting a one-day seminar on sustainable tourism. (Unit 13)
serve /sɜːv/ v. to bring food or drink to a guest at a table. e.g. We serve the main course about ten minutes after the starter. (Unit 5)
settle the bill /ˌsetl ðə ˈbɪl/ phr. to pay all the money you owe, especially at the end of a stay. e.g. Lucía settled the bill and asked for a taxi to the airport. (Unit 4)
sightseeing /ˈsaɪtsiːɪŋ/ n. the activity of visiting famous and interesting places. e.g. We do some sightseeing every afternoon after lunch. (Unit 1)
signature /ˈsɪɡnətʃə/ n. your name written by hand at the bottom of a document. e.g. Could I have your signature on the invoice, please? (Unit 4)
signpost /ˈsaɪnpəʊst/ n. a sign by the road that shows directions and distances. e.g. Follow the signposts to the city centre. (Unit 6)
smoke detector /ˈsməʊk dɪˌtektə/ n. a small device on the ceiling that makes a loud noise when there is smoke. e.g. A smoke detector is fitted in every guest room of the resort. (Unit 14)
spacious /ˈspeɪʃəs/ adj. large, with a lot of room to move around. e.g. The family suite is spacious enough for five people. (Unit 2)
speak up /ˌspiːk ˈʌp/ phr. to talk more loudly so that the other person can hear you. e.g. Could you speak up a little? The line is very bad. (Unit 8)
special offer /ˌspeʃl ˈɒfə/ n. a reduced price or extra benefit that is available only for a short time. e.g. The resort has a special offer this month: four nights for the price of three. (Unit 12)
square /skweə(r)/ n. an open public space in a town, often with buildings around it. e.g. The walking tour starts in the main square at nine o'clock. (Unit 6)
starter /ˈstɑːtə/ n. a small dish served at the beginning of a meal. e.g. She ordered tomato soup as a starter. (Unit 5)
suite /swiːt/ n. a large, expensive hotel room with separate areas for sleeping and sitting. e.g. The honeymoon suite has got a balcony with a sea view. (Unit 2)
switchboard /ˈswɪtʃbɔːd/ n. the central telephone system of a company that connects callers to different people or departments. e.g. Aziza works on the hotel switchboard from nine to five. (Unit 8)
taboo /təˈbuː/ n. something that a culture or religion does not allow people to do or talk about. e.g. In the host family's home, refusing bread is a serious taboo. (Unit 11)
take a message /ˌteɪk ə ˈmesɪdʒ/ phr. to write down information from a caller for somebody else. e.g. He's in a meeting right now. Can I take a message? (Unit 8)
take the first turning /teɪk ðə fɜːst ˈtɜːnɪŋ/ phr. to turn into the first street on your left or right. e.g. Take the first turning on the left after the bridge. (Unit 6)
target audience /ˈtɑːɡɪt ˌɔːdiəns/ n. the particular group of people a company wants to sell its product to. e.g. The target audience for our yurt camp is young adventure travellers. (Unit 12)
tipping /ˈtɪpɪŋ/ n. the practice of giving extra money to somebody for good service. e.g. Tipping is expected in American restaurants but optional in many other countries. (Unit 11)
tour guide /ˈtʊə ɡaɪd/ n. a person who shows visitors around famous places and tells them about local history. e.g. Our tour guide tells wonderful stories about the old city. (Unit 1)
tour operator /ˈtʊər ˌɒpəreɪtə/ n. a company or person that plans and organises package holidays for groups. e.g. The tour operator organises a ten-day trip along the Silk Road. (Unit 1)
tourist /ˈtʊərɪst/ n. a person who travels to a place for pleasure. e.g. Thousands of tourists visit Khiva every spring. (Unit 1)
towering /ˈtaʊərɪŋ/ adj. extremely tall and rising high above everything around. e.g. The towering minaret can be seen from every part of the old town. (Unit 10)
trade fair /ˈtreɪd feə/ n. a large event where companies from one industry exhibit their products. e.g. We are presenting our new booking app at the trade fair in Dubai. (Unit 13)
travel agent /ˈtrævl ˌeɪdʒənt/ n. a person who helps customers choose and book their holidays. e.g. The travel agent books our flights and hotel rooms. (Unit 1)
tray /treɪ/ n. a flat object used for carrying plates, cups and glasses. e.g. He balanced six glasses of juice on one tray. (Unit 5)
turn right /tɜːn raɪt/ phr. to change direction towards the right side. e.g. Turn right at the bank and the hotel is in front of you. (Unit 6)
twin room /ˌtwɪn ˈruːm/ n. a hotel room with two single beds for two guests. e.g. The colleagues booked a twin room to share the cost. (Unit 2)
UNESCO site /juːˈneskəʊ saɪt/ phr. a place officially protected by UNESCO because of its cultural or natural importance. e.g. Itchan Kala in Khiva was declared a UNESCO site in 1990. (Unit 10)
unforgettable /ˌʌnfəˈɡetəbl/ adj. so wonderful or special that you will always remember it. e.g. The hot-air balloon ride over the valley was truly unforgettable. (Unit 12)
upgrade /ˈʌpɡreɪd/ n. a change to a better room, seat or service, often at no extra cost. e.g. Loyal guests sometimes receive a free upgrade to a suite. (Unit 12)
upgrade /ˈʌpɡreɪd/ v. to give a guest a better room or seat for the same price. e.g. They upgraded us to a suite with a balcony. (Unit 7)
urgent /ˈɜːdʒənt/ adj. needing attention immediately. e.g. Mark the message as urgent because the guest's flight leaves today. (Unit 8)
vegetarian /ˌvedʒəˈteəriən/ adj. not containing meat or fish; describing a person who does not eat them. e.g. The chef prepared a vegetarian plov without any meat. (Unit 5)
venue /ˈvenjuː/ n. the place where an event happens. e.g. The riverside hotel is a popular venue for product launches. (Unit 13)
voicemail /ˈvɔɪsmeɪl/ n. an electronic system that records spoken messages from callers. e.g. If nobody answers, please leave a voicemail after the tone. (Unit 8)
voucher /ˈvaʊtʃə/ n. a piece of paper that you can use instead of money. e.g. The manager gave us a dinner voucher for the rooftop restaurant. (Unit 7)
waiter /ˈweɪtə/ n. a person whose job is to serve food and drinks in a restaurant. e.g. Our waiter recommended the chef's special plov. (Unit 5)
wake-up call /ˈweɪk ʌp kɔːl/ n. a telephone call from reception that wakes a guest at a fixed time in the morning. e.g. Shall I arrange a wake-up call for half past six? (Unit 4)
walking tour /ˈwɔːkɪŋ tʊə/ n. a tour of a place that a group does on foot with a guide. e.g. Our walking tour of the old town starts at nine o'clock sharp. (Unit 9)
well-preserved /wel prɪˈzɜːvd/ adj. kept in good condition over a long period of time. e.g. The city walls are remarkably well-preserved after six centuries. (Unit 10)
witness /ˈwɪtnəs/ v. to see an accident or incident happen. e.g. A porter witnessed the fall and called for help immediately. (Unit 14)

REFERENCES

The design of A Complete Guide to Tourism English rests on three complementary strands of language-teaching scholarship. The first is the communicative approach, which treats language above all as a tool for getting things done: checking a guest in, calming a delayed passenger, recommending a dish, closing a booking. The second is task-based learning, in which grammar and vocabulary are encountered, practised and recycled inside meaningful workplace tasks — role-plays, telephone calls, emails and itineraries — rather than in isolated drills. Throughout the units, form-focused work is always anchored to a communicative outcome that a tourism professional would recognise from a real shift.

The third strand is English for Specific Purposes (ESP), and in particular its insistence on needs analysis. Following the learning-centred tradition established by Hutchinson and Waters and refined by Dudley-Evans and St John, every unit in this book begins from the question what will learners actually have to do in English at work? The target situations of front-desk, food-and-beverage, guiding, transport and travel-agency contexts were used to select lexis, functions and text types, while CEFR descriptors guided the grading of tasks and the can-do self-assessment lists. The works below shaped that methodology and are recommended to teachers who wish to adapt the material to their own learners.

Basturkmen, H. (2010). Developing courses in English for specific purposes. Palgrave Macmillan.

Council of Europe. (2001). Common European Framework of Reference for Languages: Learning, teaching, assessment. Cambridge University Press.

Council of Europe. (2020). Common European Framework of Reference for Languages: Learning, teaching, assessment — Companion volume. Council of Europe Publishing.

Dann, G. M. S. (1996). The language of tourism: A sociolinguistic perspective. CAB International.

LESSON PLANS

The fourteen plans in this section give teachers a ready-made 50-minute lesson for each unit of the book, following a lead-in → presentation → controlled practice → freer practice → feedback sequence. Timings are suggestions: stretch or shorten stages to suit your group, and always set the unit Hometask writing activity so that classroom language is consolidated at home. Anticipated problems are listed with quick classroom solutions so that you can plan your monitoring before the lesson begins.

UNIT 1 Introduction to the Tourism Industry 50 min

Aims — by the end of the lesson, students can:

  • name the main sectors of the tourism industry and key job titles;
  • describe a tourism professional’s duties and daily routine using the Present Simple;
  • ask and answer simple questions about work in tourism.

Target language: Present Simple for describing jobs and routines (third-person -s, questions, negatives); sector and job vocabulary (tour operator, travel agent, concierge).

Materials: Coursebook Unit 1, board, job-title cards or slips, photos of four tourism workplaces.

Procedure:

  • Lead-in (5 min): Show photos of an airport, a hotel lobby, a restaurant and a museum, and elicit every tourism job students can connect to each picture.
  • Presentation (10 min): Tell the class about a hotel receptionist’s typical day (“She starts at 7 a.m., she greets guests…”) and use it to board the Present Simple forms, the third-person -s and question word order.
  • Controlled practice (15 min): Students complete the Unit 1 verb-form and gap-fill exercises about tourism workers’ routines, then compare answers in pairs before open-class checking.
  • Freer practice (15 min): In pairs, students draw a job card each and interview one another in role (“What do you do every morning?”), then report their partner’s routine to another pair.
  • Feedback & wrap-up (5 min): Correct the third-person -s slips collected while monitoring and elicit three new job titles learned in the lesson.

Anticipated problems and solutions:

  • Students drop the third-person -s → use a silent finger-correction signal and a short choral drill of “he checks / she books”.
  • Learners confuse travel agent and tour operator → concept-check with simple definitions (“Who sells the holiday? Who builds it?”).
  • Mixed levels in interviews → pair a stronger speaker with a weaker one and give the weaker student the question card.

Homework: Set the Unit 1 Hometask writing activity — “A Day in the Life of a Tourism Professional” (8–12 sentences about one job from the unit, using the template).

UNIT 2 Hotel Types and Accommodation 50 min

Aims — by the end of the lesson, students can:

  • describe hotel types and facilities with appropriate adjectives;
  • use there is / there are and have / has got to talk about what a hotel offers;
  • compare accommodation options with comparatives and superlatives.

Target language: Adjectives for describing places; there is / there are; have / has got; comparative and superlative forms.

Materials: Coursebook Unit 2, board, pictures of a resort, a hostel, a guesthouse and a boutique hotel.

Procedure:

  • Lead-in (5 min): Display the four accommodation pictures and have students rank them from cheapest to most expensive, justifying each choice with one adjective.
  • Presentation (10 min): Build a board profile of an imaginary hotel (“There are two pools, it has got a spa, it is bigger than the guesthouse…”) and chart the comparative and superlative formation rules underneath.
  • Controlled practice (15 min): Students complete the Unit 2 gap-fill with there is/are and have/has got, then transform sentences to compare two hotels from the unit.
  • Freer practice (15 min): Pairs invent “the best hotel in town” and present it in one minute using at least three facilities and two superlatives.
  • Feedback & wrap-up (5 min): Run delayed correction of comparative errors heard during presentations and finish with a quick-fire quiz (“Which is cheaper, a hostel or a resort?”).

Anticipated problems and solutions:

  • Double comparatives (“more cheaper”) → keep a visible board rule (one syllable = -er; long adjective = more) and point to it silently.
  • Confusion between there is and it has → contrast two example sentences about the same pool and concept-check the subject of each.

Homework: Set the Unit 2 Hometask writing activity — a description of your perfect hotel (8–12 sentences, following the plan in the unit).

133
UNIT 3 Making and Managing Reservations 50 min

Aims — by the end of the lesson, students can:

  • make, change and confirm a booking in a phone or email conversation;
  • choose correctly between will, going to and the Present Continuous when talking about future plans and arrangements.

Target language: Future tenses — will for spontaneous decisions, going to for intentions, Present Continuous for fixed arrangements; booking vocabulary (availability, deposit, confirmation).

Materials: Coursebook Unit 3, board, role cards with dates, room types and one change of plan.

Procedure:

  • Lead-in (5 min): Ask who has booked a hotel or ticket online and build the steps of making a reservation on the board from students’ answers.
  • Presentation (10 min): Use the unit booking dialogue to contrast “I’ll check availability” (spontaneous), “We’re going to visit Bukhara” (intention) and “We’re arriving on Friday” (arrangement) on a simple timeline.
  • Controlled practice (15 min): Students choose the correct future form in the Unit 3 exercises and reorder a jumbled reservation dialogue, checking in pairs.
  • Freer practice (15 min): Pairs role-play guest and reservations clerk using role cards that include dates, a room type and one mid-call change of plan, then swap roles.
  • Feedback & wrap-up (5 min): Replay two strong exchanges heard while monitoring and polish future-form choices with the whole class.

Anticipated problems and solutions:

  • Students use will for every future idea → ask timeline concept questions (“Did you decide now or before?”) before correcting.
  • Dates and name spelling cause breakdowns → run a one-minute alphabet and dates drill before the role-play.

Homework: Set the Unit 3 Hometask writing activity — “A trip I am going to take” (8–12 sentences about a real or imaginary trip).

UNIT 4 Check-in and Check-out Procedures 50 min

Aims — by the end of the lesson, students can:

  • manage a complete check-in and check-out conversation at a front desk;
  • make polite requests and offers with Could you…?, May I…? and Would you like…?;
  • respond appropriately to guests’ requests with polite intonation.

Target language: Polite requests and offers; front-desk vocabulary (key card, registration form, invoice, luggage storage).

Materials: Coursebook Unit 4, board, Student A / Student B role-play cards, a sample registration form.

Procedure:

  • Lead-in (5 min): Brainstorm everything a guest gives and receives at the front desk (passport, key card, receipt) onto two board columns.
  • Presentation (10 min): Work through the model check-in dialogue, underlining polite request and offer forms, and contrast the blunt “Give me your passport” with “Could I see your passport, please?”.
  • Controlled practice (15 min): Students rewrite blunt front-desk sentences as polite requests and match offers to guest situations in the Unit 4 exercises.
  • Freer practice (15 min): Pairs role-play a full check-in and then a check-out at the imaginary “Hotel Silk Road” using their A/B cards, swapping roles halfway.
  • Feedback & wrap-up (5 min): Highlight the best polite phrases overheard and drill the rising-then-falling intonation of “Would you like some help with your luggage?”.

Anticipated problems and solutions:

  • Flat intonation makes polite forms sound rude → do an exaggerated choral drill before the role-play.
  • Students mix up Could you…? and Could I…? → concept-check who performs the action in each question.

Homework: Set the Unit 4 Hometask writing activity — a blog post (8–12 sentences) about arriving and checking in at a hotel in another country.

134
UNIT 5 Food and Beverage Service 50 min

Aims — by the end of the lesson, students can:

  • take a restaurant order politely and accurately;
  • use countable and uncountable nouns correctly with some / any / much / many;
  • make polite suggestions about dishes and drinks.

Target language: Countable / uncountable nouns; some / any / much / many; polite suggestions (May I suggest…? Would you like to try…?).

Materials: Coursebook Unit 5, board, copies of a simple menu, order pads (slips of paper).

Procedure:

  • Lead-in (5 min): Run a two-minute team word race listing foods on a hotel breakfast buffet, then sort the winning list into countable and uncountable columns.
  • Presentation (10 min): Use a waiter–guest dialogue from the unit to present some / any / much / many with menu items and to highlight the suggestion phrases the waiter uses.
  • Controlled practice (15 min): Students complete the Unit 5 gap-fill with quantifiers and match polite suggestions to guest situations, checking answers in pairs.
  • Freer practice (15 min): In groups of three, one waiter takes a full three-course order from two guests and must make at least one polite suggestion, then roles rotate.
  • Feedback & wrap-up (5 min): Correct count/uncount slips such as “a bread” and have the class vote for the politest waiter of the day.

Anticipated problems and solutions:

  • Errors like “a rice” or “many money” → play a fast category-sorting game with word cards before the practice stage.
  • Menu item pronunciation blocks fluency → drill the menu chorally before the role-play begins.

Homework: Set the Unit 5 Hometask writing activity — the training-blog post “My Three Rules of Good Service” (8–12 sentences, following the plan).

UNIT 6 Giving Directions and Information 50 min

Aims — by the end of the lesson, students can:

  • give clear street directions using imperatives and prepositions of place;
  • ask for and give clarification when directions are unclear.

Target language: Imperatives for directions (go straight on, turn left); prepositions of place (opposite, next to, between); clarification phrases (Sorry, did you say left?).

Materials: Coursebook Unit 6, board, two versions of the same town map for the information gap.

Procedure:

  • Lead-in (5 min): Draw a simple street grid on the board and let students “steer” a chalk figure to a hidden café using only spoken directions.
  • Presentation (10 min): Trace a route on the unit map while presenting “Go straight on, turn left, it’s opposite the bank”, then add the clarification exchanges underneath.
  • Controlled practice (15 min): Students follow written directions to label places on the unit map and complete the prepositions gap-fill, checking in pairs.
  • Freer practice (15 min): Run a pair information gap: each student has the same map with different places marked and must ask for and give directions to complete it — speaking only, no pointing.
  • Feedback & wrap-up (5 min): Sort out the left/right mix-ups noted while monitoring and re-elicit the clarification phrases as a closing chant.

Anticipated problems and solutions:

  • Left/right confusion under pressure → attach a gesture to each word and drill them physically before the gap activity.
  • Students show their maps instead of speaking → have pairs sit back-to-back or place a folder between the maps.

Homework: Set the Unit 6 Hometask writing activity — a walking tour of your neighbourhood (8–12 sentences with at least six imperatives and four prepositions of place).

135
UNIT 7 Handling Complaints and Problems 50 min

Aims — by the end of the lesson, students can:

  • respond professionally to common guest complaints;
  • apologize with a range of set expressions and offer an appropriate solution.

Target language: Apologizing expressions (I’m terribly sorry about that; I do apologize for the inconvenience); the four-step model: listen → apologize → offer a solution → follow up.

Materials: Coursebook Unit 7, board, complaint situation cards (noisy room, wrong bill, slow service).

Procedure:

  • Lead-in (5 min): Tell a short story about a guest whose soup arrived cold, read out three possible staff replies, and have students vote on the best one and say why.
  • Presentation (10 min): Use the unit dialogue to present the four-step complaint model and board the apologizing expressions under each step.
  • Controlled practice (15 min): Students match complaints to suitable apologies and complete the Unit 7 gap-fill dialogue between an unhappy guest and the duty manager.
  • Freer practice (15 min): Pairs role-play with complaint cards, and the staff member must complete all four steps of the model before the guest may be satisfied.
  • Feedback & wrap-up (5 min): Praise the most empathetic language overheard and drill the emphatic stress in “I do apologize”.

Anticipated problems and solutions:

  • Students sound defensive or blame the guest → model “empathy first” and require an apology before any explanation.
  • The same apology is recycled every time → display a phrase menu and award a point for each different expression used.

Homework: Set the Unit 7 Hometask writing activity — an online review (8–12 sentences) about a hotel or restaurant problem, real or imagined.

UNIT 8 Telephone Skills in Tourism 50 min

Aims — by the end of the lesson, students can:

  • answer a business call professionally and transfer or hold callers politely;
  • take an accurate telephone message including names, numbers and times;
  • use repair phrases when they do not understand a caller.

Target language: Telephone phrases (I’ll put you through; Could I take a message?; Bear with me one moment); the spelling alphabet.

Materials: Coursebook Unit 8, board, blank message forms, phone-script table from the unit.

Procedure:

  • Lead-in (5 min): Read out three different call openings and have students guess what kind of tourism business is answering and what the caller probably wants.
  • Presentation (10 min): Work through the unit phone-script table, grouping phrases for answering, holding, transferring, message-taking and checking information.
  • Controlled practice (15 min): Students reorder a jumbled call, then complete a blank message form while the teacher reads a caller’s message aloud twice.
  • Freer practice (15 min): Pairs sit back-to-back and role-play two calls — booking a day tour and leaving a message for an absent manager — so they cannot rely on eye contact.
  • Feedback & wrap-up (5 min): Give feedback on clarity and name-spelling, and close with a rapid choral drill of the five most useful phrases from the lesson.

Anticipated problems and solutions:

  • Students panic without visual cues → pre-teach repair phrases (“Could you repeat that, please?”) and allow one “lifeline” per call.
  • Numbers and names are misheard → run a short alphabet-and-numbers dictation before the role-play.

Homework: Set the Unit 8 Hometask writing activity — write out a complete phone call (8–12 lines) booking a day trip to the Chimgan Mountains, using at least six phrases from the unit.

136
UNIT 9 Tour Guiding Basics 50 min

Aims — by the end of the lesson, students can:

  • structure a short guided-tour commentary with a clear beginning, middle and end;
  • use sequencing language (first, after that, finally) to guide listeners through an itinerary.

Target language: Sequencing language and itinerary phrases (Our first stop is…; After that we’ll move on to…; And finally…).

Materials: Coursebook Unit 9, board, a cut-up jumbled commentary, peer-feedback checklist slips.

Procedure:

  • Lead-in (5 min): Students recall the best excursion they have ever joined and tell a partner one thing the guide did especially well.
  • Presentation (10 min): Deliver a one-minute model commentary on the Registan, signposting each sequencing marker on the board as it is spoken.
  • Controlled practice (15 min): Groups order the cut-up jumbled commentary and insert the missing sequencing words, then check against the unit itinerary table.
  • Freer practice (15 min): Groups prepare and deliver a two-minute mini-tour of the school or town centre using at least four different sequencing markers.
  • Feedback & wrap-up (5 min): Listeners complete the peer checklist (audible? well sequenced? one interesting fact?) and the teacher offers two language upgrades per group.

Anticipated problems and solutions:

  • Guides read monotonously from full notes → allow only key-word cards during delivery.
  • Endless repetition of “then… then… then” → keep a marker menu on the board and tick each one as it is used.

Homework: Set the Unit 9 Hometask writing activity — the story of a memorable tour (8–12 sentences with at least four sequencing markers).

UNIT 10 Describing Attractions and Landmarks 50 min

Aims — by the end of the lesson, students can:

  • describe famous attractions and landmarks with factual, guidebook-style language;
  • use the passive voice (was built, is visited, can be seen) to describe places.

Target language: Passive voice for describing places, present and past; attraction vocabulary (monument, fortress, mausoleum, UNESCO site).

Materials: Coursebook Unit 10, board, photo quiz of five landmarks, blank fact-file cards.

Procedure:

  • Lead-in (5 min): Run a photo quiz of five famous landmarks (mixing world and Uzbek sites) — teams score a point for the name and another for the country or city.
  • Presentation (10 min): Present the passive through landmark facts (“The Kalyan Minaret was built in 1127; the Registan is visited by thousands of tourists”) and contrast each with its active equivalent on the board.
  • Controlled practice (15 min): Students transform active sentences into the passive and complete a fact-file gap-fill about a famous attraction in the Unit 10 exercises.
  • Freer practice (15 min): Pairs research-from-memory a local attraction, write five passive-voice facts on a fact-file card, and present it to another pair.
  • Feedback & wrap-up (5 min): Correct past-participle errors collected while monitoring and let the class vote for the most surprising fact of the day.

Anticipated problems and solutions:

  • Students attach by-agents to every sentence → show that the agent is usually omitted when it is unknown or unimportant.
  • Irregular past participles cause errors → run a one-minute drill of build–built, find–found, design–designed before practice.

Homework: Set the Unit 10 Hometask writing activity — a guidebook-style description of a famous attraction using at least five passive-voice sentences.

137
UNIT 11 Cultural Awareness and Etiquette 50 min

Aims — by the end of the lesson, students can:

  • compare cultural norms and etiquette across countries sensitively;
  • give advice to visitors using modal verbs (should, shouldn’t, must, don’t have to).

Target language: Modal verbs for advice and obligation; etiquette vocabulary (custom, taboo, hospitality, dress code).

Materials: Coursebook Unit 11, board, four etiquette statements on slips, poster paper for the tips task.

Procedure:

  • Lead-in (5 min): Read out four etiquette statements (about tipping, removing shoes, punctuality and greetings) and have students move to “agree” or “disagree” corners and defend their choice.
  • Presentation (10 min): Draw a strength scale on the board (must > should > don’t have to) and place example sentences about visiting an Uzbek home along it.
  • Controlled practice (15 min): Students choose the correct modal in the Unit 11 gap-fill about etiquette in different countries and correct a set of false advice sentences.
  • Freer practice (15 min): Groups write and present a poster, “Five Tips for Visitors to Uzbekistan”, using at least three different modal verbs.
  • Feedback & wrap-up (5 min): Clarify any must / have to / should confusion heard during presentations and pin the best tips on a class poster.

Anticipated problems and solutions:

  • Students treat should and must as identical → return to the strength scale and concept-check consequences of ignoring each.
  • Cultural generalizations become stereotypes → teach softeners such as “many people” and “it is often considered”.

Homework: Set the Unit 11 Hometask writing activity — an advice page for foreign visitors to your region, using a range of modal verbs.

UNIT 12 Promoting Tourism Services 50 min

Aims — by the end of the lesson, students can:

  • identify the persuasive devices used in tourism advertising;
  • promote a tourism service in speech and writing using persuasive language.

Target language: Persuasive language — promotional imperatives (Discover…, Escape to…), superlatives, emotive adjectives and rhetorical questions.

Materials: Coursebook Unit 12, board, two contrasting adverts for the same destination, timer for the radio-advert task.

Procedure:

  • Lead-in (5 min): Show a dull advert and a vivid advert for the same destination, have students vote for the one that makes them want to travel, and elicit why.
  • Presentation (10 min): Analyse the unit advert together, labelling each persuasive device — imperative, superlative, emotive adjective, rhetorical question — in a different colour on the board.
  • Controlled practice (15 min): Students upgrade flat sentences (“The hotel is nice”) into persuasive ones and match slogans to tourism services in the Unit 12 exercises.
  • Freer practice (15 min): Groups script and perform a sixty-second radio advert for a local tour, using at least three different persuasive devices from the lesson.
  • Feedback & wrap-up (5 min): The class votes for the most persuasive advert and must name the devices that made it work.

Anticipated problems and solutions:

  • Students borrow slogans they already know → require completely original wording and reward inventive phrases with bonus points.
  • Flat, embarrassed delivery weakens the adverts → model exaggerated “radio voice” enthusiasm before rehearsal.

Homework: Set the Unit 12 Hometask writing activity — a short promotional text for a local tourism service, using at least three persuasive devices.

138
UNIT 13 Business Tourism and Events 50 min

Aims — by the end of the lesson, students can:

  • describe business tourism and event services (conferences, exhibitions, incentives);
  • use formal language appropriately in business emails and conversations.

Target language: Formal language — fixed openings and closings (Dear Ms…, I look forward to…), full forms instead of contractions, indirect requests; MICE vocabulary (venue, delegate, catering).

Materials: Coursebook Unit 13, board, scrambled formal/informal phrase slips, model enquiry email.

Procedure:

  • Lead-in (5 min): Hand out scrambled phrase slips (“Hi guys!” vs “Dear Ms Karimova”) and have pairs race to sort them into formal and informal piles.
  • Presentation (10 min): Compare an informal and a formal version of the same conference enquiry email from the unit, highlighting the conventions that change between them.
  • Controlled practice (15 min): Students rewrite informal sentences in formal register and complete a formal reply email using the Unit 13 phrase bank.
  • Freer practice (15 min): Pairs role-play a venue coordinator and a corporate client negotiating dates, rooms and catering for a conference, keeping a consistently formal register.
  • Feedback & wrap-up (5 min): Review register slips heard during the negotiation (“gonna”, casual contractions) and elicit five formal phrases worth keeping in students’ notebooks.

Anticipated problems and solutions:

  • Register mixes mid-email (formal opening, informal body) → give a three-point checklist students apply before submitting.
  • Some learners over-correct into stiff, old-fashioned phrasing → provide a modern model email as the benchmark.

Homework: Set the Unit 13 Hometask writing activity — a formal email replying to a conference enquiry, following the unit email model.

UNIT 14 Emergency Situations and Safety 50 min

Aims — by the end of the lesson, students can:

  • give clear safety instructions to guests using imperatives;
  • warn about dangers using the First Conditional;
  • report an incident accurately in the Past Simple.

Target language: Imperatives for safety instructions (Do not use the lift); First Conditional for warnings (If the alarm sounds, staff will guide you outside); Past Simple for reporting incidents.

Materials: Coursebook Unit 14, board, safety signs or symbols, mock incident cards.

Procedure:

  • Lead-in (5 min): Show a set of hotel safety signs and have students guess what each means and where in a hotel they would expect to see it.
  • Presentation (10 min): Walk the class through a fire-drill scenario, boarding one example of each structure: an imperative (“Leave the building immediately”), a First Conditional warning (“If you smell smoke, call reception”) and a Past Simple report line (“The alarm rang at 6.40”).
  • Controlled practice (15 min): Students complete the Unit 14 First Conditional gap-fill warnings, sequence the jumbled safety announcement and supply the correct past forms in a short incident report.
  • Freer practice (15 min): Groups write and perform a one-minute safety briefing for hotel guests, then draw a mock incident card and report “what happened” to a partner in the Past Simple.
  • Feedback & wrap-up (5 min): Check conditional forms collected while monitoring (especially will appearing in the if-clause) and re-drill the clearest imperative commands.

Anticipated problems and solutions:

  • “If + will” errors persist → keep the formula If + Present Simple, … will visible on the board throughout.
  • Safety vocabulary (extinguisher, assembly point) is hard to pronounce → drill the items chorally before the briefing task.
  • Briefings become jokey → remind students that real guests must trust the speaker and grade for seriousness as well as accuracy.

Homework: Set the Unit 14 Hometask writing activity — a short incident report in the Past Simple describing what happened, what staff did and how the situation ended.
